topics.topic: How the data-directory descriptor is securely opened and whether path symlinks are refused
questions: How must the data-directory path itself be opened, and are symbolic links in that path or its ancestor components refused?
How is the data-directory descriptor itself opened, and are symbolic links in the configured data-directory path, including the final component and its ancestors, followed or refused?
May the configured data-directory path or one of its ancestors be a symbolic link, and what exact checks must acquire the held directory descriptor?

quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise, and a symbolic link found at start stops the start.

Every file the store opens itself is opened relative to the data directory it holds open from the start, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW`, never first asking whether the flag exists (A20 rule 3); a link met so later makes that store call fail with nothing written.

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
judgement.divergence: One implementer opens only the final data-directory component with no-follow semantics and permits symbolic links in ancestor components; another walks every component with `O_NOFOLLOW` and refuses such paths, which the installer and owner notice as different startup acceptance behavior.
judgement.why: The texts protect the directory itself and its contents but do not say how ancestor components of the configured data-directory path are traversed.

topics.topic: The minimum supported Linux kernel, architecture, userspace, and filesystem capabilities and behavior on unsupported hosts
questions: Which Linux kernel and filesystem capabilities are required for `O_PATH`, component-wise `O_NOFOLLOW`, namespaces, limits and bubblewrap, and what exact behavior applies on a Linux host lacking one of them?
Which Linux kernel, architecture and userspace capabilities constitute a supported host, particularly for `O_PATH`, namespace creation, resource limits and the pinned sandbox runtime?
Does “Linux” promise operation on every Linux host, or only on hosts satisfying an unstated minimum feature and architecture baseline, and how is a host below that baseline refused?

quotes: A release runs on Linux and on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18). Another host is not supported: the kernel neither tests the host nor defines what it does on another one.

Every function execution, in trial and in a run alike, runs in a fresh isolated environment created by the sandbox: Linux `bubblewrap` with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces, no network interface but the namespace's own loopback — up, as bubblewrap leaves it in a new network namespace, and reaching nothing outside the execution, so K-02's "no network" holds; this is a property of how the kernel starts bubblewrap, which the kernel does not inspect or verify at run time — the start check (rule 8) asks only that a probe execution succeeds — an environment holding only `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (rule 2), a read-only runtime, and one private exchange directory in which every file the code writes is bounded by `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` (rule 5).

ResourceBounds M04 are enforced with `setrlimit` (address space, each scratch file's size, processes), set inside the environment before the code loads and beyond the code's power to raise, and with the parent's own wall deadline and output count; how is the sandbox's own (decision 30).

Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW` — a directory on the way with `O_PATH` as well, so a directory the kernel's user may only pass through is passed; a relative path starts at the kernel's working directory; empty and `.` components are skipped, and `..` is opened as any other component — it names the parent of the directory reached so far and is never a link; the host is Linux (A20 rule 3), so no code asks whether a flag exists and there is no mode without it —, and the checks and the read use that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.
judgement.divergence: One release can claim support for every Linux architecture and kernel on which its executable starts, failing only when a required operation happens; another can impose an unstated architecture, kernel, namespace, pidfd, limit and filesystem baseline and refuse hosts below it, which installers and owners notice as different support and startup behavior.
judgement.why: Naming Linux while requiring specific Linux facilities does not define which Linux hosts are supported or a uniform refusal rule for hosts lacking those facilities.

topics.topic: Whether SQLite journal mode must be verified or forced at startup
questions: What must happen when an existing or restored SQLite database has a persistent non-default journal mode such as WAL, since the kernel neither sets the rollback mode nor defines a start check for it?
Must startup verify a particular journal mode and refuse any other mode, or may SQLite use whatever persisted or build-default mode it finds?

quotes: record_change: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] Every file and directory the module itself opens under the data directory MUST be opened relative to the data directory descriptor open_store holds, without following symbolic links, by os.O_NOFOLLOW at each component; the host is Linux (A18), so no code checks that the flag exists; a symbolic link so met by any call after start makes that call raise StoreInternalError with nothing written. The database file and every file sqlite3 creates beside it under its name, in SQLite's default journal mode left unchanged, which sqlite3 opens and cannot be told to refuse a link, are checked only by open_store before the connection opens and are not watched after it (A18).

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
judgement.why: State 7 directs the implementation to leave SQLite's journal mode unchanged and gives an exhaustive startup sequence containing no journal-mode verification or refusal.

topics.topic: Whether a failed store call may leave an unnamed published file
questions: Does "nothing written" prohibit every filesystem artifact, or only durable records, given rule 3 says a failed call may leave a published file that no record names?
If the call published a file before encountering the link, must that file be removed, or may it remain as the unnamed published file that rule 3 expressly allows a failed call to leave?

quotes: Every file the store opens itself is opened relative to the data directory it holds open from the start, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW`, never first asking whether the flag exists (A20 rule 3); a link met so later makes that store call fail with nothing written.

A call that fails writes and changes no record; the only trace it can leave is a published file no record names, which nothing reads: a spooled file is replaced at its position, value bytes are reused by equal bytes until the next start removes them (rule 4).
judgement.why: One passage requires a failed call that encounters a link to leave nothing written, while the other expressly permits a failed call to leave a published unnamed file.

topics.topic: How all store components behave if the configured data-directory pathname is renamed or replaced
questions: After the data-directory pathname is renamed or replaced, must every part of the store continue using the originally opened directory, must store calls fail, or may SQLite and the file areas resolve to different directories?

topics.topic: How configuration and credential traversal handles paths with no final component
questions: What object is checked and read when skipping components leaves no final component, as with an empty path, `.`, `/`, or paths consisting only of those components?

topics.topic: How symlinks are handled by non-open filesystem operations
questions: What happens when a symbolic link is encountered as the destination or operand of rename, unlink, stat, directory scanning or cleanup rather than by opening a file?

topics.topic: Whether configuration and credential paths must be outside the kernel private directory
questions: Is placement outside the kernel's private directory a required, checked condition, or merely an explanation of the threat, since no rule refuses a configuration or secret path inside that directory?

topics.topic: Whether replacement of the SQLite database between startup checking and opening is prevented or accepted
questions: What guarantees that the SQLite file checked at startup is the file SQLite opens, or is replacement after the scan explicitly accepted?

topics.topic: Which SQLite auxiliary files are exempt from post-start symlink checks
questions: Which exact filenames or SQLite auxiliary-file classes are exempt from post-start symlink checks as “the journal”?
